title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run declared gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; the preregistration used shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness. We present artifact‑grounded evidence (execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces), a compact evidence‑to‑claim table, a nearest‑work comparison matrix, and prescriptive preregistered protocol modifications required to obtain a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑ups.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require both correctness guarantees (reachability, policy isolation, no transient safety violations) and flexibility to express diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two architectural approaches dominate practice and recent research. Translation‑first systems constrain generation through a vendor‑aware domain specific language (DSL), apply deterministic verification and solver synthesis, and therefore prioritize provable device guarantees. Agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines centralize flexible generation in a single hosted LLM and rely on deterministic validators plus bounded repair/rollback to recover correctness while preserving generator expressivity.

This paper reports a preregistered, archived, paired experiment that asked a focused operational question: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness as measured by deterministic validator acceptance (reachability and policy isolation) — (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design (N = 120 paired tasks), the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), and a deterministic analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1).

A critical preregistered design choice shaped what the experiment measures: shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under this contract the orchestration generated one LLM candidate per task pair and supplied that identical candidate to both downstream architectures. This choice removes generator variance from the confirmatory estimand and therefore turns the experiment into a validator‑acceptance parity test for identical candidates rather than an independent assessment of generator sampling or repair efficacy. We make that limitation explicit and present artifact‑grounded evidence (execution/analysis manifests and per‑task validator traces) so readers can unambiguously interpret the observed degenerate concordance and what follow‑up protocol changes would be required to test independent generator/repair hypotheses.
sections.related_work:
Two research strands frame this study. Formal translation→verification and synthesis systems emphasize soundness and device‑level guarantees, enabling incremental checks and solver‑guided synthesis; canonical network verification work and synthesis frameworks exemplify this tradition [10,11,12]. The second strand comprises LLM‑driven NetOps and agentic AIOps research: these works investigate flexible natural‑language intent translation, multi‑tool orchestration, and iterative repair while recommending deterministic validators as guardrails to bound hallucination and unsafe proposals [3,4,5].

Nearest‑work comparison (compact matrix). We compare three representative prior works along four experimental axes (independent generation sampling, repair loop instrumentation, validator acceptance focus, emulator/hardware realism):
• INTA (ICNP 2025) [3]: independent LLM generation sampling (yes); repair loops (limited); validator acceptance (partial); emulator (yes).
• Mahmood & Song (IFIP Networking 2026) [4]: self‑correcting multi‑agent verifier pipeline (independent generation: yes; repair loops: yes; validator acceptance: emphasized; domain: Kubernetes policies/emulators).
• Weighted NetKAT / formal verification literature [5,10–12]: solver‑centric synthesis and formal guarantees (independent generation: N/A; repair loops: solver‑based; validator acceptance: core; emulator: verification models).

Positioning. The present run differs by combining preregistration, archived paired design, and deterministic per‑task validator traces under shared_initial_candidate semantics. This combination permits an auditable validator‑acceptance parity measurement for identical candidates; it explicitly does not exercise independent sampling or repair coverage.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed the primary estimand (paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness A − B), N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, declared generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, and allowed repair_iterations = 1. The preregistration, its ID, and the preregistration SHA‑256 are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract. The orchestration implemented shared_initial_candidate: a single LLM generation per task pair was produced and given identically to both translation‑first and agentic orchestration arms. This is visible in the execution manifest (planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, model_calls_used = 120) and in deterministic_reconciliation.json (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false). The execution adapter and provider audit therefore confirm adherence to the contamination controls and the preregistered generation semantics.

Task generation and difficulty metadata. Tasks were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest entry includes: intent description, initial and expected final states, a required safe sequence (ordered field changes), difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern label, required_command_count), and a canonical reference answer. Representative manifest entries (e.g., execution/task_manifest.jsonl → task‑000001 entry) and task responses (execution/responses/task‑000001‑shared‑initial.txt) are archived and show canonical reference/response alignment for many tasks.

Validator rules and scoring mechanics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies a full_intent_constraint_validation rule set: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, ordering/dependency checks (make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore patterns), final state consistency, and an explicit boolean validation_after.valid. A configuration passes end‑to‑end correctness only if validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, repair_applied flags, and score_reason_code; these files are the canonical record for scoring decisions.

Analysis executor and statistics. Analysis followed paired_binary_analysis_v1 as preregistered. Primary outputs include contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), paired difference (A − B), a bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729), and an exact McNemar two‑sided test. Analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) and deterministic_reconciliation.json document the computation and the seeds used.

Marginal success rates are baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0. The paired difference (A − B) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]; the analysis log records bootstrap_resamples = 10000 and bootstrap_seed = 1729 (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Repair outcomes and secondary estimands. Aggregated repair_applied count = 0 across all 240 episodes (execution/scoring/*.json show repair_applied = false per episode). As preregistered, secondary estimands concerning repair coverage (H2) are therefore unobserved in this execution; the artifact evidence is execution/scoring/*.json and analysis/missingness_summary.csv.

For pair‑000001 the shared candidate matches the canonical reference modulo normalization and ordering; execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json documents normalized_response == reference (normalized), parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and validation_after.valid = true. Similar representative artifacts for other pairs are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.

Contamination and missingness checks. Preregistered contamination checks produced no flags: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 120 and zero failures. Provider audit metadata in deterministic_reconciliation.json indicates cache_miss_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, supporting execution isolation and adherence to the contamination_plan.
sections.discussion:
What the experiment measured and its interpretation. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics were used by design, the confirmatory estimand realized in this run is validator‑acceptance parity: given identical LLM candidates, do the two downstream architectures differ in deterministic validator acceptance? The observed degenerate concordance (n11 = 120) shows that both validators accepted the identical candidates for every paired task. This is an unambiguous artifact‑grounded result and is precisely what the preregistered shared‑candidate protocol intended to measure: it quantifies whether orchestration differences downstream of a fixed candidate change validation outcomes. It does not, by design, test whether one architecture would generate better initial candidates or perform more successful repairs when each arm obtains independent LLM outputs.

Compact evidence‑to‑claim table (artifact‑grounded).
• H1 (Paired difference A − B in end‑to‑end correctness): Measured as validator‑acceptance parity under shared_initial_candidate; supporting artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (n11=120,n10=0,n01=0,n00=0), analysis/condition_summary.csv, execution/execution_manifest.json; verdict: tested — measured estimand = validator‑acceptance parity (not independent generator comparison).
• H2 (Agentic pipeline higher repair coverage): Not observed in this execution; supporting artifacts: execution/scoring/*.json (repair_applied=false for all episodes), analysis/missingness_summary.csv; verdict: unobserved — repair_applied counts = 0.

Nearest‑work mapping and how this run differs. The three representatives in the Related Work matrix [3,4,5,10–12] exercise different experimental axes (independent generation, active repair loops, validator emphasis). Unlike those works, the present run intentionally holds generation constant to produce a precise, artifact‑auditable validator‑parity measurement. This makes the run useful for validator regression testing and orchestrator equivalence checks but not for adjudicating generator or repair robustness under independent sampling.

Protocol recommendations for a discriminating follow‑up. To test the original broader hypotheses (independent generator and repair differences) while reusing the existing infrastructure, the preregistered modifications are: (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent initial LLM generation per pair — initial candidate model_calls would rise from 120 to 240 for the confirmatory set; (ii) enable multiple sampled generations per arm to estimate generator variance (further model‑call increase); (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied > 0 and repair coverage can be measured; (iv) optionally increase emulator fidelity or run on hardware to reduce simulator‑to‑hardware contamination risk. Each change would be reflected deterministically in the execution manifest (model_calls_used, hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair_applied flags) and is thus preregisterable and auditable.

Threats to validity (expanded). Internal validity: the shared_candidate design removes generator variance by intent; this narrows the estimand but reduces within‑pair variance. Construct validity: the deterministic validator operationalizes correctness by formalized rule checks but omits operator‑facing properties (explainability, maintainability). External validity: the corpus is synthetic and Mininet‑derived; single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single validator (v5.0) limit multi‑model generality. Conclusion validity: degenerate concordance yields a point CI and p = 1.0; these are correct descriptors of the observed data but do not imply practical equivalence under independent operation.

Reproducibility, artifact locations, and how to recompute analysis. All artifacts are archived in the run bundle and referenced by execution/execution_manifest.json. Key artifacts for reproducibility are: preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1; preregistration_sha256 recorded in the manifest), execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/responses/*, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json. The paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor parameters (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729) are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and enable deterministic recomputation of the reported CI and McNemar p using the preserved seeds and inputs.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, fully archived paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks the deterministic validator accepted the identical LLM candidates in both arms for all pairs (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false for all 240 episodes); preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage remain unobserved. The run demonstrates that preregistered shared‑candidate experiments precisely measure validator‑acceptance parity and it provides an artifactized protocol and concrete preregistered modifications that would enable a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison under independent generation and active repair in follow‑ups.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
